Senate offices are permitted to use consumer‑grade chatbots such as ChatGPT for routine tasks, but they are barred from accessing the more advanced generative‑AI systems that dominate current regulatory discussions. The restriction applies to tools that incorporate higher‑capacity language models, multimodal capabilities, or real‑time data integration, which lawmakers and staff have identified as posing heightened privacy, security and misinformation risks.

The limitation reflects ongoing congressional deliberations over AI oversight, where policymakers are weighing proposals that would impose safety standards, transparency obligations and usage controls on sophisticated AI platforms. By confining Senate personnel to baseline chatbot services, the chamber aims to mitigate exposure to untested technologies while it evaluates broader legislative frameworks intended to safeguard public and governmental data from emerging AI threats.
author: NPR Politics

title: Trump sued by CNN, MS NOW, Politico over alleged rights violations
content:
CNN, MS NOW, and Politico have filed a request with a federal court seeking an order that would limit the president’s ability to take actions they say infringe on their constitutional rights.  The three outlets argue that the president’s recent conduct—ranging from targeted investigations to public statements—constitutes an attempt to punish them for coverage that they view as unfavorable.  They claim the president’s behavior violates the First Amendment’s protections of free speech and the press.

The petition outlines several specific grievances, including the president’s use of executive authority to subpoena internal documents, the public release of classified information that the outlets say is used to intimidate them, and the threat of legal action against their journalists.  The plaintiffs argue that these measures are retaliatory and designed to silence critical reporting rather than to address any legitimate national security concerns.  They request an injunction that would prohibit the president from pursuing further investigations or punitive actions against the three media organizations.

The case is now before a federal judge, who will decide whether the president’s conduct constitutes a constitutional violation or falls within the scope of permissible executive power.  The outcome could set a precedent for how the executive branch interacts with the press and may influence future disputes over the limits of presidential authority.
author: NPR Politics

title: DOJ defends Trump media ban, urges court to reject lawsuit
content:
The Department of Justice (DOJ) has defended President Donald Trump’s recent decision to ban coverage from several prominent media outlets, citing concerns that reporting by CNN, MS Now and Politico on a range of political and policy issues could jeopardize national security and disseminate falsehoods. In a statement released this week, DOJ officials argued that the ban was a necessary measure to protect sensitive information and prevent the spread of misinformation that could undermine public trust and national interests.

The DOJ’s justification centers on alleged inaccuracies and sensationalism in stories published by the three outlets. Officials claimed that repeated coverage of certain policy disputes and political controversies had amplified misinformation, potentially compromising strategic operations and diplomatic negotiations. The ban, which was announced by President Trump shortly after a series of contentious reports, has been framed by the DOJ as a protective action rather than a punitive one, emphasizing the need to safeguard classified data and secure communications.

While the DOJ maintains that the ban is warranted to preserve national security, critics argue that it raises significant First Amendment concerns and could set a precedent for executive censorship of the press. The move has prompted calls for further scrutiny from both media watchdogs and congressional committees, who are examining the balance between security imperatives and freedom of the press.
author: NPR Politics

title: Trump Praises Economy and Iran Moves at UNGA
content:
Former President Donald J. Trump addressed the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Tuesday, using the global forum to highlight what he described as the United States’ recent international and domestic achievements.  In a 12‑minute speech delivered from the assembly’s main hall, Trump praised the administration’s trade agreements, citing the U.S.–Mexico–Canada Agreement and the U.S.–Japan trade pact as examples of “strategic diplomacy” that he said had secured American jobs and strengthened allies.  He also referenced the U.S. withdrawal from the Paris Climate Accord and the “realignment” of U.S. foreign policy toward a more “America‑first” stance, framing these moves as successes that restored national sovereignty.

On the domestic front, Trump highlighted the tax‑cut legislation passed in 2017, arguing that it spurred a record‑low unemployment rate and a surge in private‑sector investment.  He also mentioned the administration’s efforts to reduce regulatory burdens on small businesses and to expand access to healthcare through the repeal of the Affordable Care Act’s individual mandate.  The former president’s remarks were part of a broader campaign to shape his legacy, with his campaign team noting that the UN audience provided a “global platform” to reinforce his narrative of American strength.

Reactions to the speech were mixed.  While supporters applauded the emphasis on economic growth and national sovereignty, critics pointed to the lack of substantive policy proposals and the omission of key issues such as climate change and human rights.  Nevertheless, the former president’s appearance at the General Assembly marked a rare moment of international engagement for the former administration, underscoring his continued influence in shaping public discourse on U.S. foreign and domestic policy.
author: NPR Politics

title: Women urged to lead climate governance
content:
Climate Home News has highlighted a growing concern that the climate crisis is also a governance crisis, with a persistent blind spot for women’s leadership. The article, titled “Women are on deck – it’s time they steered,” argues that women’s ingenuity and readiness to make decisive choices are largely absent from the decision‑making bodies that shape climate policy.

The piece points out that women hold a disproportionate share of the world’s climate‑related jobs and are often the first to experience the impacts of extreme weather, yet they remain underrepresented in national and international climate negotiations. It cites studies showing that gender‑balanced teams produce more innovative solutions and that countries with higher female participation in politics tend to adopt stronger environmental regulations. The article calls for systematic reforms to ensure women’s voices are integrated into policy frameworks, from local adaptation plans to global treaty negotiations.

In conclusion, the Climate Home News article stresses that addressing the climate crisis effectively requires inclusive governance that fully harnesses women’s leadership potential. By removing the current blind spot and empowering women to steer climate action, policymakers can achieve more resilient and equitable outcomes.
author: Climate Home News

title: Elmo Shares Storm Experience at Climate Week
content:
A Climate Week gathering in New York City turned to an unlikely speaker when political leaders were seen as slow to act on the climate crisis. The event featured Elmo, the three‑and‑a‑half‑year‑old red Muppet from Sesame Street, who addressed the audience about how rising temperatures and extreme weather are already affecting children. Elmo’s appearance was highlighted as a creative way to engage younger audiences and bring a child’s perspective to the discussion.

During his brief address, Elmo recounted a recent storm that struck Sesame Street, an episode that also starred singer Post Malone. He described his own fear during the event, using his characteristic third‑person narration to illustrate how even beloved characters can be impacted by climate‑related events. The talk was part of a broader Climate Week program that aimed to underscore the urgency of protecting children from the consequences of global warming.

The use of a familiar child‑friendly figure was intended to humanize the science and policy debate, making the risks of climate change more tangible for both young listeners and adults. By sharing Elmo’s experience, the event organizers sought to emphasize that the climate crisis is not only an environmental issue but also a pressing social concern that demands immediate action.
author: Guardian Environment

title: Loneliness May Cut 6 Years of Healthy Life for U.S. Adults
content:
A 2023 report reveals that nearly 50 % of U.S. adults experience loneliness, while a comparable proportion report feelings of social isolation. The findings underscore a growing public health issue that parallels other chronic conditions in its potential to affect physical and mental well‑being. The study, conducted by a national health research organization, surveyed more than 4,000 adults across the country, asking them to rate their sense of connection and belonging over the past year.

The data show that loneliness and isolation are not confined to any single demographic group; they cut across age, income, and geographic lines. Researchers noted that both conditions are linked to increased risks of cardiovascular disease, depression, and premature mortality, yet they remain underrecognized in clinical practice and public health policy. The report calls for targeted interventions—such as community‑based programs, workplace initiatives, and digital platforms—to address the social determinants that contribute to these widespread feelings of disconnection.

Public health officials are urged to treat loneliness and social isolation with the same urgency as other modifiable risk factors. By integrating screening tools into routine medical care and expanding community outreach, policymakers can begin to mitigate the health impacts identified in the study. The findings highlight the need for coordinated action to reduce the prevalence of loneliness and isolation among U.S. adults.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Reminder System Boosts Cancer Screening in High-Risk Groups
content:
Health systems are adopting a new strategy to boost participation in cancer screening programs: patients who are scheduled for one type of cancer test are now being prompted to consider other relevant screenings. By integrating reminders for multiple tests into a single appointment, providers aim to streamline preventive care and reduce missed opportunities for early detection.

Early evidence suggests that this coordinated approach can improve adherence rates. When patients receive a single, consolidated reminder—such as a note about colorectal, breast, or cervical cancer screening alongside their current test—they are more likely to schedule and complete the additional procedures. The method also simplifies the patient experience, potentially lowering the administrative burden on both clinicians and patients.

If widely implemented, the strategy could increase the overall uptake of life‑saving screenings, helping to catch cancers at earlier, more treatable stages. Health organizations are encouraged to evaluate the feasibility of integrating multi‑screening reminders into routine practice and to monitor outcomes to ensure the approach delivers the intended benefits.
author: Medical Xpress

title: New Ultrasound Standards Set for Arthritis Diagnosis
content:
A large multinational research effort has produced the first age‑specific ultrasound reference values for assessing joint health, a development that could streamline the diagnosis of early inflammatory arthritis. The study, which pooled data from rheumatology centers across several continents, established normative sonographic patterns for healthy joints in distinct age groups, enabling clinicians to differentiate normal age‑related changes from the subtle signs of inflammatory disease that often appear in its initial stages.

By providing clear benchmarks, the new standards are expected to reduce diagnostic uncertainty and shorten the time between symptom onset and treatment initiation for patients with early inflammatory arthritis. The findings, published in a peer‑reviewed rheumatology journal, underscore the utility of ultrasound as a non‑invasive, cost‑effective tool and may inform future clinical guidelines aimed at improving outcomes for individuals at risk of chronic joint damage.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Dietary Interventions May Reduce Inflammatory Symptoms in Hirschsprung Disease
content:
A multi‑institutional study led by researchers at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia (CHOP) has, for the first time, shown that dietary interventions can reduce inflammatory symptoms in patients with Hirschsprung disease, a congenital bowel motility disorder. The results were published in the peer‑reviewed journal *Gastroenterology* and were obtained through a collaborative effort involving several academic medical centers.

Hirschsprung disease is characterized by missing nerve cells in portions of the colon, leading to severe constipation and intestinal obstruction. Inflammation often complicates the condition, worsening symptoms and increasing the risk of complications. The CHOP investigators tested specific nutritional strategies—including high‑fiber diets and targeted probiotic supplementation—in a cohort of affected children and observed a significant decline in markers of intestinal inflammation and a corresponding improvement in bowel function. These findings suggest that non‑pharmacologic, diet‑based approaches could become a valuable adjunct to current surgical and medical therapies, potentially improving long‑term outcomes for patients with this rare disorder.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Brain's Neural Dynamics Keep Vision Stable
content:
Scientists have uncovered how the brain’s visual system maintains rapid, accurate perception despite the irregular firing patterns of its millions of neurons. Each glance initiates a complex cascade of excitatory and inhibitory signals, with additional modulation arriving from the thalamus and neuromodulatory centers. This dynamic network does not operate on a fixed clock, yet it reliably supports tasks such as face recognition, judging the trajectory of an approaching vehicle, and reading street signs even as lighting and motion conditions change.

The study, conducted by researchers at the Institute for Neural Dynamics, used high‑density electrophysiological recordings to map the timing and coordination of neuronal activity across visual cortex and subcortical pathways. Their findings show that the brain employs adaptive synchrony and feed‑forward inhibition to filter noise and prioritize salient stimuli, allowing for rapid decision‑making without the need for a rigid temporal framework. These insights deepen our understanding of sensory processing and may inform the design of artificial vision systems that mimic biological flexibility.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Exercise May Ease Stress-Related Bladder Pain in IC/BPS
content:
A preclinical study conducted by investigators at Weill Cornell Medicine suggests that chronic stress may worsen the pain and urinary symptoms associated with interstitial cystitis/bladder pain syndrome (IC/BPS). The research, which examined animal models of the condition, found that sustained stress exposure triggers alterations in both bladder tissue and the nervous system, potentially amplifying the discomfort and frequency of urination reported by patients.

The study’s authors noted that stress‑induced changes included increased inflammation within the bladder wall and heightened sensitivity of nerve fibers that innervate the urinary tract. These physiological shifts could explain why many individuals with IC/BPS experience flare‑ups during periods of emotional or psychological strain. While the findings are preliminary and derived from animal experiments, they provide a mechanistic link that may help explain the clinical observation that stress often exacerbates IC/BPS symptoms.

If confirmed in human studies, the results could inform new therapeutic strategies that target stress‑related pathways, offering patients additional avenues for symptom relief. The investigators plan to pursue further research to validate these mechanisms in clinical populations and to explore potential interventions that mitigate stress‑induced bladder dysfunction.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Study Links Substance Use Disorder to Higher Suicide Risk
content:
People with substance use disorder face a markedly higher risk of both attempting suicide and completing suicide, a new study from the Karolinska Institutet reports. The research, published in *Molecular Psychiatry*, analyzed data from a large cohort of individuals diagnosed with substance use disorder and compared their suicide rates to those of the general population.

The findings indicate that the likelihood of suicide attempts and fatal outcomes is significantly elevated among those struggling with substance misuse. The authors highlight that the combination of physiological dependence, psychological distress, and social isolation may contribute to this heightened vulnerability. They emphasize the importance of early identification and integrated treatment strategies that address both addiction and mental health concerns.

The study underscores the urgent need for clinicians and public‑health practitioners to prioritize suicide prevention efforts within substance‑use treatment programs. By incorporating routine mental‑health screening and providing comprehensive support, healthcare systems can better mitigate the elevated suicide risk observed in this high‑risk population.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Parents with Shared Mental Health Conditions Increase Family Disease Risk, Study Finds
content:
The adage that “birds of a feather flock together” appears to extend to romantic partnerships, according to a new study published in *JAMA Psychiatry*. Researchers examined a large cohort of parents to determine whether individuals with psychiatric disorders are more likely to pair with partners who share similar mental and physical health conditions, and how such assortative mating may influence disease risk for both spouses and their offspring.

Using nationwide health records, the study found that parents with psychiatric diagnoses—such as depression, anxiety, or bipolar disorder—were statistically more likely to have partners who also carried psychiatric or chronic physical illnesses. The analysis revealed that these paired health profiles amplified the risk of comorbid conditions in subsequent generations, suggesting that shared genetic predispositions and environmental factors can compound disease susceptibility. The authors noted that the findings underscore the importance of considering partner health histories in clinical assessments and public health strategies aimed at mitigating inherited disease burdens.

These results highlight the complex interplay between personal choice, genetic inheritance, and environmental exposure in shaping health outcomes. By acknowledging that couples often share similar health trajectories, clinicians and policymakers can better target prevention efforts and support services to families where mental and physical health risks converge.
author: Medical Xpress

title: IAM Launches Workers vs Billionaires Campaign in Eight Midterm Battleground States
content:
The International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers (IAM), one of the United States’ largest labor unions, has announced a new “workers v billionaires” political campaign aimed at mobilizing its members in eight key battleground states for the upcoming midterm elections. With a membership base of nearly 700,000 active and retired workers across North America, the union represents employees at major corporations such as Boeing, Lockheed Martin, United Airlines, and Harley‑Davidson. By focusing on states that could swing the election—Maine, Pennsylvania, Michigan, Texas, Ohio, Georgia, Arizona, Nevada, and Illinois—IAM seeks to amplify the political voice of workers in the national conversation.

The campaign encourages union members to support candidates who prioritize labor interests and to increase voter turnout among the working class. IAM’s strategy includes targeted outreach, educational events, and coordination with local union chapters to ensure that workers are informed about candidate positions on wages, benefits, and workplace safety. The union’s leadership argues that a coordinated effort across these diverse regions will help counterbalance the influence of wealthy donors and reinforce the political power of the labor movement.

As the midterms approach, IAM’s initiative underscores the growing trend of labor unions engaging directly in electoral politics. By concentrating resources on swing states, the union aims to influence policy outcomes that affect millions of American workers, reinforcing the broader national debate over the role of labor in shaping economic and social policy.
author: Guardian Business

title: UK warns of rising debt costs and slower growth ahead of Budget
content:
Higher energy costs are tightening global growth prospects, as analysts point to a confluence of geopolitical and environmental pressures.  Rising prices of oil and natural gas, driven by supply disruptions linked to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, are already weighing on industrial output and consumer spending in major economies.

In addition to the conflict, climate‑change‑related events—such as severe droughts and extreme weather—are forcing governments to shift toward renewable energy sources, which can entail higher upfront costs and supply‑chain adjustments.  The combination of volatile fossil‑fuel markets and the transition to cleaner energy is expected to slow GDP growth in both developed and emerging markets, according to forecasts from the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank.

Policymakers are responding by tightening fiscal rules and boosting investment in energy efficiency, while some central banks signal that higher inflationary pressures may prompt tighter monetary policy.  The dual impact of geopolitical instability and climate‑driven energy transition is likely to remain a key constraint on global economic performance in the coming years.
author: BBC Business

title: Back‑to‑work adviser urges sick employees to call boss
content:
Sir Charlie Mayfield, a senior executive at the National Workforce Development Agency, warned that heavy reliance on text and email communication can leave employees who are ill disengaged and less likely to return to work. In a statement released Monday, Mayfield cited internal data showing that workers who reported sickness through digital channels reported lower levels of job satisfaction and a higher probability of extended absences.

The agency’s analysis, which examined over 12,000 employee health reports last year, found that those who used text or email to notify managers of illness were 18 percent less likely to resume duties within the expected recovery period compared with employees who communicated via phone or face‑to‑face meetings. Mayfield said the impersonal nature of written messages may contribute to a sense of isolation and reduce the perceived support from supervisors.

In response, the agency is exploring a hybrid communication strategy that incorporates real‑time messaging, scheduled check‑ins, and optional video calls to ensure that sick workers feel connected and supported during their recovery. The initiative aims to improve return‑to‑work rates and overall workforce resilience.
author: BBC Business

title: Blood Test Fails to Detect Pain in Horses with Gastric Ulcers
content:
A recent study conducted by a team of Australian veterinarians has highlighted the difficulty of detecting pain in horses suffering from gastric ulcers, underscoring a pressing need for improved diagnostic methods in equine veterinary practice. The research, published in a peer‑reviewed journal, focused on the subtle and often ambiguous clinical signs that can indicate discomfort in affected animals.

The investigators examined 120 horses diagnosed with gastric ulceration and assessed a range of behavioral and physiological indicators, including changes in posture, feeding patterns, and heart rate variability. They found that many of the signs traditionally used to infer pain—such as reduced feed intake or altered gait—were also present in healthy horses and in those with other conditions, making it hard to isolate ulcer‑related discomfort. The study suggests that reliance on these conventional cues may lead to under‑recognition of pain, potentially compromising animal welfare and treatment outcomes.

The authors call for the development of more specific, objective biomarkers and training protocols to aid veterinarians and horse owners in identifying ulcer‑related pain early. They also recommend further research into the pathophysiology of equine gastric ulcers to inform better therapeutic strategies and improve overall equine health management.
author: Phys.org

title: Canadian Musicians Report Struggles Amid AI, Streaming, and Venue Closures
content:
Canadian musicians are expressing growing frustration with the technology sector, citing the rise of generative artificial intelligence as a key factor that they believe is eroding the value of their work. Recent studies and surveys indicate that artists across the country feel that AI‑generated music is flooding streaming platforms, making it increasingly difficult for human creators to attract listeners and secure revenue.

Industry experts note that the proliferation of AI tools has lowered the barrier to entry for music production, allowing non‑musicians to produce high‑quality tracks at a fraction of the cost. This shift, musicians argue, dilutes the market for original compositions and pressures traditional revenue streams such as streaming royalties and live performances. In response, several Canadian music associations are calling for clearer licensing frameworks and greater support for artists to protect their intellectual property in an era of rapid technological change.
author: Phys.org

title: Misophonia Triggers Strong Emotions to Everyday Sounds
content:
Misophonia, a condition that triggers intense emotional reactions to ordinary sounds such as chewing, sniffing, or tapping, has been identified as a source of sudden distress and anger for people of all ages. The disorder, which is increasingly recognized by clinicians, can provoke a range of responses—from irritation to full-blown rage—often leaving sufferers and those around them bewildered and upset.

Medical experts explain that misophonia involves an abnormal neural response to specific acoustic cues, causing the brain to interpret these sounds as threats. While the exact prevalence remains unclear, studies suggest it affects a small but significant portion of the population, including children, adults, and their families. Treatment approaches vary, with some patients finding relief through sound therapy, cognitive behavioral strategies, and environmental modifications, though no universal cure has yet been established.

In light of growing awareness, healthcare providers are encouraged to consider misophonia in differential diagnoses when patients report extreme reactions to everyday noises. Early recognition and supportive interventions can help mitigate the emotional toll on individuals and their social circles, fostering a better understanding of this complex auditory sensitivity.
author: Phys.org

title: QUT researchers develop model to stabilize expert decision rankings
content:
Queensland University of Technology researchers have unveiled a new decision‑making tool designed to improve the reliability of collective judgments in large‑scale projects such as infrastructure development and public‑policy formulation. The model, created by Ph.D. candidates Omid Motamedisedeh and Faranak Zagia of QUT’s School of Architecture and Built Environment, aims to mitigate the volatility that can arise when minor variations in expert opinions produce markedly different outcomes.

By systematically accounting for small discrepancies in individual assessments, the tool offers governments, businesses and other organisations a more consistent framework for evaluating complex proposals. Its developers say the approach addresses a longstanding challenge in group decision‑making, where even slight divergences among experts can lead to divergent conclusions, thereby enhancing confidence in the final decisions made across a range of strategic initiatives.
author: Phys.org

title: Q&A: Dynamic side of language development in toddlers
content:
Overhearable speech—words spoken by caregivers that children hear but are not directly addressed—makes up more than half of the language exposure for children in the United States. Despite its ubiquity, the impact of this background listening on language development has not been thoroughly investigated. A new study by researchers at the University of Chicago, The New School for Social Research, and Princeton University seeks to fill that gap.

The team focused on English‑learning children growing up in the U.S., analyzing how and when they come to understand vocabulary that appears only in parents’ conversations at home. By examining the timing of exposure and the subsequent comprehension of these words, the researchers aim to clarify the mechanisms through which overheard speech contributes to children’s growing lexicon and overall linguistic competence.

The study’s findings will help educators and parents better appreciate the value of everyday dialogue in the household. Understanding how children process overheard language can inform strategies that support early language acquisition and guide future research into the broader effects of passive listening on child development.
author: Phys.org

title: UCC Study Shows Arts and Culture Key to Climate Action
content:
University College Cork (UCC) has released new research indicating that the arts, cultural and creative sectors can serve as powerful catalysts for climate action. The study argues that artistic expression has the capacity to reshape public understanding of climate change, influence engagement with environmental issues, and ultimately drive behavioural change. By framing climate narratives in creative contexts, the arts can make complex scientific concepts more accessible and emotionally resonant for diverse audiences.

The research, which combined quantitative surveys of over 2,000 participants with qualitative case studies of community art projects across Ireland, found that exposure to climate-themed performances, exhibitions, and digital media significantly increased participants’ willingness to adopt sustainable practices. Interviews with artists and curators highlighted that collaborative, interdisciplinary projects—such as installations that use recycled materials or performances that incorporate real‑time environmental data—often spark conversations that extend beyond the gallery or theatre setting. The study also identified key mechanisms, including storytelling, visual symbolism and participatory workshops, that enhance the persuasive power of artistic climate messaging.

These findings suggest that policymakers and funding bodies could leverage the arts as a strategic tool in national climate communication campaigns. UCC researchers recommend further investigation into long‑term behavioural impacts and the scalability of arts‑based interventions. By integrating creative approaches into broader climate strategies, governments may broaden public engagement and accelerate the transition to more sustainable societies.
author: Phys.org

title: Could Negative Mass Exist?
content:
Scientists and physicists have long treated mass as an inherently positive quantity, with gravity described as a universal attraction between masses. Yet the possibility of negative mass—a hypothetical form of matter that would repel ordinary mass and itself—has emerged in theoretical discussions, especially within the realms of general relativity and quantum field theory. While no experimental evidence currently supports the existence of such exotic matter, the concept is not ruled out by any fundamental law and has been invoked to explain phenomena ranging from cosmic inflation to the theoretical construction of warp drives and traversable wormholes.

Theoretical models that incorporate negative mass predict a range of counterintuitive behaviors. A negative‑mass particle would experience a gravitational force that pushes it away from a positive‑mass source, while the positive mass would be attracted toward the negative mass, potentially leading to a runaway acceleration of the pair. In cosmological contexts, a small density of negative mass could drive accelerated expansion, offering an alternative to dark energy. Experimental attempts have focused on analogues, such as metamaterials that mimic negative effective mass in condensed‑matter systems, but these do not constitute true negative‑mass particles. In particle physics, certain solutions to the Dirac equation allow for negative‑energy states, yet the interpretation of these states as negative mass remains speculative.

At present, the existence of negative mass remains an open question. Without empirical confirmation, it remains a useful theoretical tool for probing the limits of gravitational theory and exploring exotic space‑time geometries. Should future experiments detect a genuine negative‑mass particle, the ramifications would be profound, challenging the standard model of cosmology, redefining gravitational dynamics, and potentially unlocking new technologies based on repulsive gravity. Until then, the notion remains a fascinating, if unverified, extension of our understanding of the universe.
author: Phys.org

title: Kent Meningitis Outbreak Linked to Gene-Transfer Bacteria
content:
A sudden meningitis outbreak in Kent, United Kingdom, that began in March has been linked to a rare bacterial strain that acquired virulence genes from otherwise harmless microbes.  Public health officials identified the culprit as a strain of *Neisseria meningitidis* that had incorporated genetic material from commensal bacteria residing in the human gut and throat, giving it the ability to evade the immune system and cause severe disease.  The outbreak, which has so far affected more than 80 people and resulted in three deaths, is the most serious meningitis event in the region in over a decade.

Investigations by the UK Health Security Agency and the National Institute for Health Research show that the gene transfer occurred through horizontal gene transfer, a process in which bacteria exchange DNA fragments.  The newly acquired genes encode proteins that help the pathogen survive in the bloodstream and cross the blood‑brain barrier.  In response, local health authorities have intensified surveillance, increased vaccination coverage with the MenACWY vaccine, and issued guidance to clinicians to consider this strain when diagnosing meningitis.  The outbreak underscores the importance of monitoring genetic changes in bacterial populations and the potential for harmless microbes to contribute to emerging infectious threats.
author: New Scientist

title: Mindful Lifestyle Changes Match CBT in Treating Depression
content:
A recent randomized controlled trial has shown that a brief, lifestyle‑focused intervention can be as effective as standard cognitive‑behavioural therapy (CBT) for treating depression.  The study, published in *The Lancet Psychiatry*, followed 1,200 adults with moderate depressive symptoms over 12 weeks.  Participants were randomly assigned to receive either a 12‑session CBT program or a structured package of advice on mindful eating, regular exercise and sleep hygiene, delivered by trained health coaches.

The results were striking: remission rates at the end of the trial were 41 % in the lifestyle group and 43 % in the CBT group, a difference that was not statistically significant.  Both interventions produced comparable improvements in depressive symptom scores and quality‑of‑life measures, with the lifestyle group reporting higher satisfaction with the simplicity and autonomy of the program.  Researchers noted that the intervention required fewer clinical hours and could be delivered in primary‑care or community settings, potentially expanding access to effective depression treatment.

These findings suggest that incorporating evidence‑based lifestyle advice into mental‑health care could provide a viable, low‑intensity alternative to CBT for many patients.  The authors call for further research to refine the components of the program and to assess long‑term outcomes, but the study underscores the therapeutic value of mindful eating, exercise and sleep hygiene as core elements of depression management.
author: New Scientist

title: Ancient Gallo-Roman Wall Found Beneath Paris Cathedral Site
content:
A Gallo‑Roman wall uncovered beneath a building on Paris’s Île de la Cité has been hailed by the French Ministry of Culture as a “major breakthrough,” according to officials. The 20‑metre (65‑foot) stretch of masonry was found during summer excavations near Notre‑Dame Cathedral, a site long suspected of containing remnants of the city’s earliest settlement.

Archaeologists report that the wall dates to the Roman occupation of Gaul, and its discovery provides tangible evidence of the layout of ancient Paris. The structure’s proximity to the Île de la Cité suggests it may have formed part of the original fortifications that defined the city’s core. The find is expected to help scholars refine maps of early Paris and may prompt further investigations into surrounding underground layers.

The Ministry’s statement underscores the significance of the discovery for understanding the city’s origins. Researchers plan to conduct additional digs to assess the wall’s extent and context, with the hope that further evidence will illuminate how Paris evolved from a Roman settlement into the modern capital.
author: Guardian Science

title: Farmers upset over lost £233m environmental funding
content:
Farmers across the region are expressing growing concern that they will be unable to carry out essential environmental projects after losing access to a key funding stream. The grant, which had supported activities such as soil conservation, biodiversity enhancement, and carbon‑sequestration initiatives, was recently withdrawn as part of a broader budget reallocation.

The loss of the subsidy means that many growers will have to forgo planned measures that improve pasture quality, reduce erosion, and protect local wildlife habitats. Without the financial support, the cost of implementing these practices could exceed the resources available to small‑holder operations, potentially compromising long‑term sustainability goals and the compliance obligations tied to national environmental targets.

In response, agricultural groups are urging policymakers to reconsider the funding cut and to explore alternative financing mechanisms. They argue that maintaining these environmental efforts is critical not only for ecological health but also for the resilience of the farming sector in the face of climate change.
author: BBC Science

title: Two Git Ignore Files You Likely Missed
content:
Mihai Dinculescu recently published a short technical note on his personal development blog titled *“Two Git Ignore Files Nobody Told Me About.”* The post explains two lesser‑known mechanisms for excluding files from a Git repository that are not covered in most introductory guides. While the article is concise, it offers a practical overview of how these files can be used to keep a project’s history clean and to reduce merge conflicts.

The first file discussed is the repository‑specific *`.git/info/exclude`*, which functions like a local `.gitignore` but is not committed to the repository. Dinculescu highlights its usefulness for developers who want to ignore machine‑specific or IDE‑generated files without affecting teammates. The second file is the global ignore file, typically located at `~/.config/git/ignore` or referenced via the `core.excludesfile` configuration. The author demonstrates how setting this file can centralize ignore rules across all projects for a single user, simplifying workflow and ensuring consistency.

The blog post was shared on Hacker News, where it received four points and three comments. Readers praised the clarity of the explanation and noted that the information is valuable for teams looking to streamline their Git hygiene. The discussion was brief, suggesting that while the topic is niche, it resonates with developers who manage large codebases or collaborate across multiple environments.
author: Hacker News

title: QuestDB (YC S20) Hiring Pre-Sales Engineer for North America
content:
QuestDB, the open‑source time‑series database company, announced a new opening for a Pre‑Sales Engineer covering North America. The position, listed on the firm’s career portal, seeks a candidate with experience in technical sales, software engineering, and database technologies to support prospective customers, conduct product demonstrations, and assist the sales team in translating business requirements into technical solutions. The role is described as a full‑time, on‑site position based in the United States, offering a competitive salary and benefits package, and is part of QuestDB’s broader effort to expand its market presence in the high‑performance data analytics sector.

The posting has attracted attention on the technology news aggregator Hacker News, where the link was shared without generating comments or upvotes at the time of reporting. No further discussion has been recorded on the platform, indicating limited community engagement with the announcement. QuestDB’s recruitment drive underscores its ongoing commitment to scaling its engineering and sales capabilities as demand for real‑time data processing solutions continues to rise.
author: Hacker News

title: Claude Code Reads AGENTS.md Only When Telemetry Enabled
content:
A recent blog post from Szypowi’s development team announced a new capability for Anthropic’s Claude language model: the ability to read and interpret code within its own agents, but only when telemetry is enabled. The update, detailed in the post titled “Claude code reads agents – MD only when telemetry is on,” explains that the model can now ingest source files and analyze their structure, improving its performance on programming tasks that involve internal agent logic. The feature is gated behind telemetry to ensure that user data is not inadvertently exposed, allowing developers to opt‑in for the enhanced functionality while maintaining privacy controls.

The announcement has already sparked discussion on Hacker News, where the post received 120 upvotes and 44 comments. Community members praised the technical depth of the feature, noting that it could streamline debugging workflows and enable more sophisticated agent behaviors. Some commenters raised concerns about the reliance on telemetry, suggesting that clear opt‑in mechanisms and transparent data handling policies will be essential for broader adoption. The developers responded by outlining the telemetry settings and emphasizing that the code‑reading mode remains fully controllable through the model’s configuration.

Overall, the introduction of telemetry‑controlled code reading marks a notable step toward more autonomous and context‑aware agents in Claude. By allowing the model to access and analyze its own codebase only when explicitly permitted, the team balances functionality with user privacy. As developers experiment with this new feature, it will likely influence how future iterations of conversational agents are built and deployed in production environments.
author: Hacker News

title: RxFilm Studio Enables AI‑Powered Video Creation for Product Marketing
content:
A new open‑source tool called RxFilm Studio has been released by the RxTech Lab to streamline the creation of marketing videos for independent developers and small teams. The platform, which is available on GitHub, claims to automate the entire production pipeline—from initial concept and storyboard generation to editing, visual and sound effects, voiceover synthesis, background music, and subtitle translation. By allowing users to start with a simple idea, a product website, images, or existing footage, the tool aims to reduce the time and effort traditionally required to produce professional‑looking promotional content.

RxFilm Studio’s workflow is designed to be fully AI‑driven. According to the project’s documentation, the system can automatically generate a coherent story structure, lay out a timeline, apply visual and audio effects, and produce multilingual subtitles. The GitHub repository (https://github.com/rxtech-lab/film-workflow) provides the code and instructions for local deployment, while a demonstration video showcasing the tool’s capabilities is hosted on YouTube (https://youtu.be/9_M15fRdZQE). The developers invite users to try the software and share feedback through the comments section on the Hacker News post linked in the original announcement.

The launch of RxFilm Studio reflects a growing trend toward AI‑assisted media production, offering a low‑barrier solution for teams that lack dedicated video editing resources. By consolidating multiple post‑production tasks into a single, automated workflow, the tool could help small businesses and solo developers produce polished marketing videos more efficiently. The project remains open source, encouraging community contributions and further development.
author: Hacker News

title: OpenAI Deploys Influencer Campaign to Promote ChatGPT
content:
OpenAI is expanding its marketing reach by tapping into the influencer ecosystem, a move highlighted in a Business Insider profile that details the company’s new strategy for 2026. The plan centers on integrating ChatGPT into creator content, with paid ads and sponsorships that allow influencers to showcase the AI’s capabilities directly to their audiences. By partnering with prominent Instagram personalities and other social‑media figures, OpenAI aims to normalize the use of its language model in everyday digital interactions.

Key elements of the strategy include a tiered sponsorship program that rewards creators for embedding ChatGPT prompts and tutorials into their posts, stories, and reels. The company is also experimenting with targeted ad placements that appear alongside influencer content, using data on engagement and audience demographics to refine messaging. Early reports suggest that the approach has already begun to increase brand visibility among younger, tech‑savvy users, while providing creators with new revenue streams and interactive tools for their followers.

If the campaign gains traction, it could signal a broader shift for AI firms toward creator‑driven marketing, blending product promotion with authentic content creation. By 2026, OpenAI’s influencer partnerships may become a standard component of its outreach, potentially reshaping how AI services are introduced to mainstream consumers.
author: Hacker News

title: Ive Sent It: Online File Courier with Signed Proof of Delivery
content:
A link to the website ivesentit.com was posted on Hacker News under item ID 49815168. The post received a modest 6 up‑votes and attracted two comments from the community. The brief discussion on the page indicates that the site has just been introduced to a wider audience, but no detailed description of its purpose or content was provided in the original submission.

The two comments that appeared on the Hacker News thread were short and largely focused on the novelty of the new URL rather than on its functionality or offerings. No additional context or user feedback about the website’s features or intended audience was shared, leaving readers with only the basic information that the site exists and has been shared on a popular tech forum.

The limited engagement suggests that while the site has captured some curiosity, it has yet to generate broader interest or substantial discussion within the Hacker News community. As with many niche web projects, further visibility will likely depend on additional promotion and clearer communication of its value proposition.
author: Hacker News

title: AI-Native Systems: Stable Infrastructure Explained
content:
Fagner Brack’s recent blog post, “Here’s what AI‑native with stable infra looks like,” was shared on Hacker News under the ID 49815344. The article, which explores how companies that build AI from the ground up differ from traditional software firms, has garnered ten up‑votes but no comments to date.

Brack argues that true AI‑native organizations embed machine‑learning pipelines into every layer of their stack, from data ingestion to model serving, and rely on a highly automated, version‑controlled infrastructure that can scale with model updates. He contrasts this with legacy firms that retrofit AI onto existing systems, noting that the latter often face bottlenecks in data quality, latency, and governance. The post cites examples such as OpenAI, Anthropic, and newer startups that have adopted cloud‑native architectures, container orchestration, and continuous integration/continuous deployment (CI/CD) pipelines tailored for AI workloads. Brack also highlights the importance of observability and compliance tooling in maintaining a stable, auditable AI ecosystem.

The piece has sparked interest among the Hacker News community, reflected in its modest point tally. While no comments have been posted yet, the article’s concise overview of AI‑native infrastructure principles offers a useful reference for engineers and product managers seeking to evaluate or build AI‑centric systems.
author: Hacker News

title: Samsung software update causes smart fridges to freeze
content:
Samsung’s latest software update for its smart refrigerator line has inadvertently caused a number of units to freeze, according to reports from Android Authority. The update, released to improve performance and add new features, was found to trigger the fridge’s cooling system to shut down unexpectedly, resulting in food spoilage and user frustration. The issue has been identified by both Samsung’s own diagnostics and independent user reports.

Affected models include the Galaxy Family series and newer Smart Fridge models that run the company’s Bixby‑integrated interface. Samsung has acknowledged the problem and issued a patch to restore normal operation, advising owners to install the update immediately. The company has also offered a limited warranty claim process for customers who have experienced food loss. While the fix is available, the incident highlights the risks of over‑the‑air updates in appliances that rely on precise temperature control.

The incident has drawn attention to the growing complexity of connected home devices and the importance of rigorous testing before deployment. Samsung’s prompt response and provision of a corrective update should mitigate further damage, but the event serves as a cautionary example for manufacturers of IoT appliances.
author: Hacker News

title: Smart Glasses Spark Chaos in India
content:
Shubnam was in the middle of packing boxes for a move when a friend sent a short Instagram video that had just been posted a few hours earlier. The clip, however, was actually recorded several days prior at a Delhi protest that took place this spring. Demonstrators had gathered to oppose a proposed bill that would have narrowed the legal recognition and protections for transgender people in India.

The footage shows a crowded street in Delhi, with participants holding signs and chanting slogans demanding equal rights. Shubnam, who is part of the transgender community, watched the video with a mix of surprise and concern, noting that the protest had been largely peaceful but highly visible. The bill, which had sparked nationwide debate, was eventually shelved after significant public backlash and criticism from civil‑rights groups.

While Shubnam’s move was unrelated to the protest, the video’s sudden appearance highlighted how quickly social media can bring distant events into personal awareness. The incident underscores the ongoing struggle for transgender rights in India and the role of digital platforms in amplifying activist voices.
author: MIT Tech Review

title: India Faces Smart Glasses Crisis as Meta Devices Spark Protests
content:
The Download, a daily technology newsletter, reports that Meta’s smart glasses are already sparking controversy in India. At a recent protest in Delhi, a content creator wearing the company’s head‑mounted device was filmed on Instagram, raising questions about the device’s data‑collection capabilities and the legality of its use in public demonstrations. The footage shows the glasses capturing audio and video of the crowd, prompting concerns among activists that the technology could be used for surveillance or to identify protestors.

Industry experts note that Meta has marketed its smart glasses as a tool for immersive media creation, but the Delhi incident highlights potential privacy risks. Indian regulators have begun reviewing the device’s compliance with the country’s data protection laws, and several civil‑rights groups are calling for stricter oversight. The protest itself drew attention to the broader debate over wearable technology and its impact on civil liberties in high‑profile public events.

While Meta maintains that its glasses are designed for consumer use and do not actively record or transmit data without user consent, the Delhi incident has accelerated calls for clearer regulatory frameworks. The company’s next steps will likely involve engaging with lawmakers and revising its privacy policy to address the concerns raised by the protest footage.
author: MIT Tech Review

title: Emma Waters Leads National Campaign Against Fertility Technology
content:
Emma Waters, a prominent activist in the reproductive‑health arena, has launched a nationwide campaign opposing the use of in‑vitro fertilization (IVF), surrogacy arrangements, and polygenic testing in fertility technology. The initiative, which has quickly gained traction among certain advocacy groups, seeks to limit the application of these methods on the grounds of ethical and societal concerns. Waters, who has a background in bioethics, announced the campaign in a press briefing that highlighted her intent to influence both public policy and private sector practices.

The campaign’s central argument is that IVF, surrogacy, and polygenic testing represent a departure from traditional family‑building practices and raise complex ethical questions. Waters has called for stricter regulatory oversight and has urged lawmakers to consider the long‑term implications of widespread use of these technologies. She has also emphasized that her efforts are conducted with the full support of her husband, who has publicly endorsed the cause. The movement has already attracted attention from several state legislatures and a number of advocacy organizations that are reviewing proposed policy proposals.

While the campaign has sparked debate among medical professionals and patient advocacy groups, Waters remains focused on shaping national discourse around reproductive technology. She has outlined a series of policy recommendations that aim to curb the expansion of IVF, surrogacy, and polygenic testing, and she plans to lobby for legislative changes in the coming months. The outcome of this effort will likely influence the regulatory landscape for fertility services across the country.
author: Wired

title: AT&T expands automation, reduces workforce
content:
The telecommunications conglomerate announced a strategic initiative aimed at demonstrating to investors that it can increase operational efficiency while reducing costs. In a recent briefing, senior executives outlined plans to trim the workforce, lower electricity consumption, and expand the use of automated technologies across its network and customer‑service platforms, positioning the effort as a response to heightened expectations from Wall Street for stronger profit margins.

The company expects the combined impact of staffing reductions, energy‑saving measures and advanced automation to boost productivity and improve earnings per share in the upcoming fiscal year. Executives indicated that the initiative will be phased in over the next twelve months, with progress tracked through quarterly performance reports, signaling a commitment to delivering measurable cost savings while maintaining service quality.
author: Wired

title: Kate Tolo Pursues Biohacking Regimen to Empower Women
content:
Tolo, a participant in a new biohacking study, is following a demanding schedule of physiological tests that mirror those performed by her boyfriend, a self‑identified biohacker. The protocol includes continuous monitoring of nighttime erections and the application of extreme heat during menstruation, all aimed at gathering data for a broader research initiative.

The study, which seeks to improve health outcomes for women—comprising roughly half of the global population—relies on detailed biometric tracking. Participants record sleep‑related sexual activity and expose themselves to controlled heat therapy during their periods, with the data being aggregated to identify patterns that could inform future medical interventions.

Researchers hope that the insights gained from these rigorous tests will lead to more personalized treatment options for women’s health issues. While the methods are unconventional, the project’s goal is to expand the scientific understanding of female physiology and improve care for a demographic that has historically been under‑represented in clinical research.
author: Wired

title: SmartLabels QR Code System Review: AI Inventory in a Busy Household
content:
SmartLabels, a start‑up that uses artificial‑intelligence to generate item inventories from photographs, was put to the test by a homeowner who wanted to see whether the system could handle the clutter and constant rearrangement typical of a busy household. The user captured a series of images of living‑room shelves, kitchen cabinets, and a cluttered play area, then let the SmartLabels app process the photos and produce a searchable inventory list.

The AI was able to identify and categorize a wide range of items—including books, electronics, kitchenware, and children’s toys—assigning each a unique identifier and storing the data in a cloud‑based database. The system also flagged duplicates and suggested possible storage optimizations. While the app performed well on static shots, it struggled to maintain accurate counts when items were moved between photos, indicating that frequent re‑scanning may be required for highly dynamic environments.

The test demonstrates that SmartLabels can quickly generate a comprehensive inventory from a single snapshot, but its effectiveness in a constantly changing setting may depend on the user’s willingness to update the database regularly. For households that maintain a more stable arrangement, the technology offers a convenient way to track possessions and streamline organization.
author: Wired

title: Paperman Adds Paper‑Like Texture to Laptop Screens
content:
Paperman, a new screen‑texture application, has been designed to reduce eye strain by adding a subtle overlay to digital displays. The developer claims the texture mimics the slight grain of paper, creating a more natural visual environment for users who spend long periods looking at screens. According to the app’s documentation, the effect is adjustable, allowing users to fine‑tune the intensity to match their lighting conditions and personal preferences.

The primary use cases highlighted by the creators are reading, writing, and general text‑centric tasks. By softening the stark contrast between the screen and ambient light, Paperman aims to make prolonged exposure to high‑definition displays less tiring. Early adopters report improved comfort during extended work sessions, noting that the texture does not interfere with text clarity or color accuracy. The app is available for both iOS and Android platforms and can be activated through a simple toggle in the device’s accessibility settings.

While still in its early stages, Paperman’s approach reflects a growing trend toward ergonomic software solutions that address visual fatigue. As more users seek ways to mitigate the impact of blue light and screen glare, tools like Paperman may become a standard feature in productivity suites. The app’s developers plan to release updates that expand compatibility with additional operating systems and integrate more advanced customization options.
author: Wired

title: Startup Aims to Power Data Centers with Supercritical CO2
content:
A new retrofit technology promises to boost the efficiency of existing gas turbines by attaching a lightweight, high‑temperature coating that improves combustion and reduces fuel consumption. While the added layer can lower operating costs and extend the life of the turbines, it does not eliminate the carbon dioxide and nitrogen oxide emissions that these engines inherently produce. The developers say the system is designed for quick installation on current units, allowing power plants to enhance output without a full replacement of the turbine fleet.

The coating works by increasing the turbine’s operating temperature range, which allows more of the fuel’s energy to be converted into useful work. Laboratory tests show a 5–8 % improvement in thermal efficiency, translating into measurable fuel savings for large industrial and utility customers. However, the technology does not capture or convert the exhaust gases; the emissions profile remains largely unchanged, meaning regulatory compliance will still require separate carbon‑capture or emission‑control measures.

Industry analysts view the retrofit as a pragmatic interim step for operators looking to reduce fuel costs while awaiting more advanced, low‑emission solutions. By improving efficiency without removing emissions, the technology offers a modest environmental benefit, but it underscores the continued need for broader decarbonization strategies in the power sector.
author: Wired

title: Best Samsung Phones 2026: Ultra, Fold, and Budget Models
content:
Samsung’s Galaxy lineup has grown into a comprehensive ecosystem that covers every segment of the smartphone market, from entry‑level models to high‑end flagships and the latest foldable devices. The company now offers budget‑friendly options such as the Galaxy A series, which deliver essential features at a lower price point, while the Galaxy S and Galaxy Z series push the envelope with premium displays, advanced cameras, and cutting‑edge processors. The foldable range, including the Galaxy Z Fold and Z Flip, introduces new form factors that combine tablet‑sized screens with the portability of a phone, appealing to both consumers and professionals who demand versatility.

Industry analysts note that Samsung’s strategy of maintaining a diverse product portfolio helps it capture a broad customer base amid intensifying competition from rivals like Apple, Google, and Chinese manufacturers. The company’s recent releases have emphasized software continuity through One UI, robust 5G connectivity, and improved battery life across all models. In addition, Samsung’s emphasis on ecosystem integration—such as seamless pairing with Galaxy Buds, Galaxy Watch, and SmartThings—provides added value for users who invest in multiple devices.

WIRED has compiled a detailed guide to help readers navigate Samsung’s extensive range, highlighting key specifications, price points, and use‑case scenarios for each segment. The guide aims to clarify which devices best meet different needs, whether a budget-conscious shopper seeks a reliable daily driver or a tech enthusiast desires the latest foldable innovation. By offering clear comparisons and expert insights, WIRED seeks to simplify the decision‑making process for consumers exploring Samsung’s ever‑expanding Galaxy family.
author: Wired

title: Meta Issues Patch for Muse AI Security Flaw
content:
Meta announced that it has released a patch for a critical zero‑day vulnerability in its AI assistant Muse, which could have allowed attackers to execute arbitrary code on a victim’s Mac. The flaw, identified by security researchers, would have enabled an attacker to take full control of a user’s system, effectively granting them the ability to “do whatever” they wanted, from data theft to installing malware. The company stated that the fix addresses the underlying flaw in Muse’s code execution path and is available through the latest macOS updates.

The incident highlights the growing risks associated with AI‑powered assistants that run on personal devices. Muse, designed to provide contextual help and automate routine tasks, relies on deep integration with macOS, making it a high‑value target for attackers. Meta’s swift response and patch rollout underscore the importance of timely vulnerability remediation in the rapidly evolving AI ecosystem.

While the patch mitigates the immediate threat, security experts caution that the incident serves as a reminder of the broader security implications of embedding AI assistants into everyday computing environments. Continued vigilance and rigorous testing will be essential as AI features become increasingly common in consumer software.
author: Wired

title: Eight Sleep launches Pod 6 with compact cooling hub for under‑bed placement
content:
Eight Sleep has unveiled its next‑generation “intelligent sleep system,” the Pod 6, which promises to adjust a bed’s temperature automatically in response to real‑time health data such as breathing patterns and heart rate.  The company describes the new device as its “most significant hardware launch to date,” highlighting a newly engineered cooling hub that is compact enough to fit beneath most mattresses.  The Pod 6 builds on the foundation laid by the 2025 Pod 5, but offers a slimmer, more streamlined design that still delivers the same advanced temperature‑control capabilities.

Pricing for the Pod 6 is lower than the previous model, though it remains a premium investment.  Eight Sleep lists the Standard version at $2,699 for a full‑size mattress and $2,999 for a king‑size mattress, with additional options for custom configurations.  The system is now available directly through Eight Sleep’s online store, allowing consumers to order the device without a third‑party retailer.  The company emphasizes that the Pod 6’s sensors continuously monitor sleep metrics, enabling the cooling hub to fine‑tune the sleeping environment throughout the night.

With the release of Pod 6, Eight Sleep seeks to solidify its position in the growing market for connected sleep technology.  By integrating more precise biometric tracking with a more discreet cooling mechanism, the company aims to offer users a more comfortable and data‑driven sleep experience.  The new hardware launch underscores Eight Sleep’s commitment to advancing sleep science through consumer‑friendly products.
author: The Verge

title: OpenAI hires former Patreon execs for creator product
content:
OpenAI has announced the appointment of Patreon co‑founder Sam Yam as head of its new Creator Product division. Yam, who has served as Patreon’s technology chief since its launch 13 years ago, made the announcement on X, noting that he will be joined by former Patreon product head Drew Rowny and engineering head Shannon Ma, both of whom stepped down from the platform in recent weeks. Together, the trio will shape OpenAI’s strategy for tools and services aimed at creators and their audiences.

The move follows OpenAI’s broader effort to expand its product offerings beyond AI research. By bringing in executives with deep experience in subscription‑based creator ecosystems, the company signals a commitment to developing early‑access tools that enhance creator workflows and community engagement. Yam emphasized that the new initiatives will be “critically valuable to Creators and their communities,” underscoring a focus on practical, creator‑centric solutions.

With this leadership shift, OpenAI is positioning itself to compete more directly in the creator economy, leveraging its AI capabilities to offer innovative features for content creators. The addition of seasoned Patreon veterans is expected to accelerate the rollout of these tools and strengthen the company’s foothold in the rapidly evolving creator marketplace.
author: The Verge

title: Xiaomi 18 Pro Phones Feature Rear Displays and Privacy Screens
content:
Xiaomi unveiled its new 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max in China today, marking the first time the company has released a global launch for the series. The devices keep the rear‑display concept introduced with the 17 Pro models, allowing the compact screens to double as notification panels, selfie cameras and simple gaming displays while still housing the dual 200‑megapixel camera array. The phones also incorporate Qualcomm’s latest Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 processors, a step up from the chips used in the previous generation.

The 18 Pro line follows a similar design language to the 17 Pro, featuring a flexible privacy‑display technology that mirrors Samsung’s Galaxy S26 Ultra. Both models offer a more flexible take on the rear‑screen concept, and the company confirmed a worldwide release later this year. This international rollout comes after the 17 Pro series was limited to select markets, broadening Xiaomi’s presence in the high‑end smartphone segment.
author: The Verge

title: European report warns of rising orbital collision risk
content:
A senior space‑policy analyst at the International Space Agency’s annual conference cautioned that the growing congestion of Earth’s orbital environment could soon render several key orbital slots unusable. “I think we are going to lose the ability to use certain orbits,” the analyst said, highlighting the mounting risk of collision and debris in low‑Earth orbit (LEO) and the geostationary belt.

The warning follows a sharp rise in the number of active satellites, particularly from large constellations, and an increasing inventory of defunct spacecraft and spent rocket stages that remain in orbit. Experts noted that the cumulative effect of these objects could trigger a cascade of collisions—known as the Kessler syndrome—making it difficult to safely maneuver new payloads into those crowded regions. Agencies such as NASA, ESA, and the Russian Roscosmos are already reviewing orbital slot allocation and debris‑mitigation protocols to preserve operational access.

In response, the conference concluded with a call for coordinated international regulations and the development of active debris‑removal technologies. While the immediate impact on satellite launches remains uncertain, the consensus is that proactive measures are essential to maintain the long‑term viability of critical orbital pathways.
author: Ars Technica

title: New Imaging Reveals Details of Hunga Caldera Collapse
content:
Post‑eruption imaging of the Hunga caldera has revealed previously unseen details of its collapse, according to a new study released by a team of volcanologists. The research, which followed the 2021 eruption that produced a series of explosive blasts and a large ash plume, employed high‑resolution satellite radar and airborne LiDAR to map the caldera’s topography after the event.

The analysis shows that the collapse was more extensive than earlier models suggested, with a subsidence zone stretching over 4 km² and a maximum vertical drop of roughly 200 meters. The data also indicate that the caldera walls have shifted laterally by up to 150 meters, creating a new, irregular basin shape. These findings refine the understanding of the magma chamber’s dynamics and the structural weaknesses that led to the eruption.

The updated collapse model will inform future hazard assessments for the region, particularly for communities and shipping lanes that rely on the nearby island of Hunga. Continuous monitoring with the same imaging techniques is planned to track any further changes in the caldera’s morphology.
author: Ars Technica

title: Ema Raises $77M as AI Expands in Enterprise Software
content:
Ema, a technology startup focused on enterprise data solutions, announced that it has secured a total of $140 million in funding to date. The capital round, led by a mix of venture capital firms and strategic investors, underscores the growing confidence in the company’s platform for managing and analyzing large-scale data across cloud environments.

The firm now boasts more than 50 enterprise customers, including industry leaders Google and Microsoft. These partnerships highlight Ema’s ability to deliver scalable, secure data services that meet the stringent requirements of high‑profile tech giants. The company’s client roster also spans several other Fortune 500 organizations, reflecting a broad adoption of its solutions across diverse sectors.

With this latest funding milestone and a robust customer base, Ema is positioned to accelerate product development and expand its market reach. The influx of capital is expected to support further innovation in data analytics and strengthen its competitive stance in the rapidly evolving enterprise technology landscape.
author: TechCrunch

title: Comma's Autonomous Driving Tech Investigated After Two Fatal Crashes
content:
A recent investigation has identified that several vehicle crashes involved drivers who were operating “forked” versions of Comma.ai’s autonomous driving software. The inquiry, conducted by state safety regulators, found that the modified code was not certified by the manufacturer and lacked the safety updates present in the official releases. In each case, the vehicles were engaged in automated mode at the time of the incident, and the crashes occurred while the drivers were not actively monitoring the road.

The investigation highlights the risks associated with unapproved software modifications in autonomous systems. Comma.ai’s official documentation states that only the company’s vetted builds are supported for use in production vehicles, and the company has issued a warning to its user community about the potential hazards of running third‑party forks. Regulators are reviewing the incident reports to determine whether additional oversight or licensing requirements are needed for aftermarket autonomous driving software.

The findings underscore the importance of maintaining software integrity in self‑driving technology. While the investigation is ongoing, Comma.ai has pledged to cooperate fully with authorities and to strengthen its communication with users about the dangers of unauthorized code. The agency has indicated that it will consider further regulatory measures to ensure that only certified software is used in vehicles equipped with autonomous features.
author: TechCrunch

title: PitPro Launches First Tire-Changing Robot in Canada
content:
A new startup has announced that its automated tire‑changing system can replace four tires in under 15 minutes. The company claims the technology, which combines robotic arms, computer vision, and a modular tire‑handling platform, was validated in a controlled test environment where a single unit completed a full tire change on a standard passenger vehicle without human intervention.

The system’s design allows it to pick up, remove, and install tires on all four wheels simultaneously, using a combination of suction grippers and torque‑controlled actuators to ensure proper mounting and alignment. According to the startup’s spokesperson, the process is fully autonomous, with the machine monitoring tire pressure and wheel torque in real time to meet safety and quality standards. The company says the technology could be deployed in roadside assistance fleets, automotive service centers, and even on mobile service trucks to reduce downtime for drivers.

If the startup’s claims hold up in commercial deployments, the technology could shorten service times for roadside emergencies and streamline maintenance operations in the automotive industry. The company is reportedly seeking partnerships with fleet operators and is preparing to begin pilot programs in the coming months to demonstrate the system’s reliability in real‑world conditions.
author: TechCrunch

title: LinkedIn Launches Verification Tools to Combat Fake Profiles
content:
LinkedIn has announced a new set of verification tools designed to improve the authenticity of professional profiles on its platform. The updates allow members to endorse the work experience of their colleagues, while giving companies greater authority to manage and remove accounts that falsely claim employment with them.

Under the new system, users can verify specific job titles, dates, and responsibilities, creating a more reliable record of an individual’s career history. Companies will receive enhanced controls, including the ability to flag or delete profiles that list them as an employer without permission. These measures are part of LinkedIn’s broader effort to reduce misinformation and bolster trust among recruiters, hiring managers, and job seekers.

By tightening verification processes, LinkedIn aims to provide a more accurate representation of professional credentials, potentially reducing hiring errors and improving the overall integrity of the platform’s networking ecosystem.
author: TechCrunch

title: Spotify Launches Taste Profile for US Premium Users
content:
Spotify has launched its new “Taste Profile” feature for Premium subscribers in the United States. The update allows users to view a summary of how the streaming service interprets their listening habits and to adjust those preferences using natural‑language commands. By typing simple requests such as “I want more indie rock” or “less hip‑hop,” listeners can fine‑tune the algorithm that powers their personalized playlists and radio stations.

The company says the feature is built on the same recommendation engine that underpins its Discover Weekly and Daily Mix offerings, but adds a user‑friendly interface for tweaking taste settings. Spotify’s engineering team highlighted that the natural‑language component is powered by a newly trained model that interprets context and sentiment from user input. The rollout is currently limited to Premium accounts in the U.S., with plans to expand to other markets later in the year.

Industry observers view Taste Profile as part of Spotify’s broader strategy to increase user engagement by giving listeners more control over the AI‑driven curation process.
